title: David Oyelowo and Nate Parker’s Mansa Studios Partners With Macro Television Studios to Produce Vertical Series

Macro and Mansa will develop, market and promote the projects coming out of the partnership, while also share ownership of the intellectual property. “Mansa has developed real expertise in the emerging vertical format, and we see this as an exciting opportunity to pair that experience with Maceo Television Studios’ vast capabilities across genres,” said Macro founder/CEO Charles D. title: ‘Thirteen In Gaza’ Trailer: Father & Daughter Tale Shot In Devastated Palestinian Territory Won NETPAC Award At TIFF
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘NAZA’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race View All September 21, 2026 8:41am EXCLUSIVE: Palestinian director Hosam Abu Dan’s father and daughter drama Thirteen in Gaza , set against the backdrop of the devastated Palestinian territory, won the prestigious NETPAC Award in Toronto over the weekend and Deadline can unveil the international trailer. The film, which world premiered in TIFF ’s Centrepiece sidebar, was shot entirely in Gaza with local Palestinian cast and crew under wartime conditions. It is the first feature-length local production to come out of Gaza since the beginning of the Israeli military campaign, sparked by the October 7, 2023 terror attacks, which has killed close to 74,000 people, injured more than 173,000 people and reduced much of the territory to rubble. Related Stories Festivals 'La Bola Negra' Wins Oscar-Predictive Toronto Film Festival People's Choice Award Reviews 'Magazine' Review: Lily McInerny And Bright Young Cast Give Flavor To Pre-Digital Vanishing Era Of NY's Literary World - Toronto Film Festival Mary Ziyara stars as 13-year-old Ragha who lost her home and most of her family in a missile attack in the Gaza Strip, opposite Firas Al-Masri as her father. Watch on Deadline The pair eke out a life in a crowded displacement camp, with Ragha navigating puberty without safety, privacy and her mother, while her father faces hard choices to ensure their survival. Abu Dan was unable to make the trip to Toronto for the premiere. The festival left their allocated front row seats empty and the director addressed the audience via a pre-recorded video address. “Honestly I wish I could have been with you in this moment… to have watched the film on the big screen, to see the birth of Thirteen in Gaza , a film I can only compare to my first child,” he said against the backdrop of a pile of rubble. “For it to be born while I am far from it, it’s a hard feeling.” Abu Dan emphasized the fact the film had been shot in Gaza with an entirely local cast and crew, noting the production had overcome obstacles at every turn. “One of the hardest situations is that on the fourth day a nearby strike hit us and one of our colleagues was seriously injured,” he said. “After that I started asking myself what it means to have a drama come out of Gaza after a long war and a long absence of dramas coming out of Gaza. Then I realized this film was made with blood.” It is the first feature film for Abu Dan after short film Six Miles Out and documentary Gaza Sound Man. The production was made with the support of the Doha Film Institute and the Arab Culture Fund. Mad World handles international sales. title: James Sloyan, Actor in ‘The Sting,‘ ‘Xanadu’ and ‘Oh Madeline,’ Dies at 85
full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 8:37am James Sloyan Carsey-Werner / Courtesy Everett Collection James Sloyan, the busy character actor who appeared in films including The Sting and Xanadu and played Madeline Kahn’s husband on her short-lived 1980s ABC sitcom, has died. He was 85. Sloyan died July 22 at his home in Sherman Oaks, his family announced over the weekend. Star Trek fans know him for his five appearances as a member of four species across The Next Generation , Deep Space Nine and Voyager in the 1990s, and he served as the voice of Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus in commercials for 18 years starting in 1989. Related Stories Music Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist, Dies at 45 Movies Gerrit Graham, Actor in 'Phantom of the Paradise,' 'Pretty Baby' and 'Used Cars,' Dies at 77 In George Roy Hill’s The Sting (1973), winner of the Oscar for best picture, Sloyan helped set the plot in motion with his turn as Mottola, the numbers runner who works for racketeer Doyle Lonnegan (Robert Shaw) and falls victim to a “pigeon drop scam” perpetrated by Johnny Hooker ( Robert Redford ) and Luther Coleman ( James Earl Jones ). And in the Olivia Newton-John musical fantasy Xanadu (1980), he played Simpson, the tyrannical boss of Michael Beck’s artist Sonny Malone at AirFlow Records. Sloyan landed the role of Kahn’s husband, a guy who writes steamy romance novels under the pen name Crystal Love, but the 1983-84 show — the first produced by Carsey-Werner Productions — lasted just 18 episodes. The youngest of four kids, James Joseph Sloyan was born in Indianapolis on Feb. 24, 1941. His father, James Sr., was a construction engineer. When he was 4, he “discovered the delights of the Indianapolis State Fair, wrangling an appearance with [Western movie actor] Lash LaRue and his traveling Western Show,” his family said. After spending time living overseas and in Albany, New York, Sloyan graduated from the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York and served three years in the U.S. Army before returning to New York, where he acted and was a choreographer for fight scenes for Joseph Papp’s New York Shakespeare Festival. He made it to Broadway in Arthur Kopit’s Indians in 1969, had the lead in such off-Broadway productions as Irv Bauer’s A Dream Out of Time and made his onscreen debut in the 1970 film The Traveling Executioner , starring Stacy Keach. Sloyan, who moved to California in 1973, appeared in The Gang That Couldn’t Shoot Straight (1971) and on episodes of The Doctors , The Streets of San Francisco , Kojak and Delvecchio before landing a regular role on the 1977 ABC drama Westside Medical . He played a Romulan admiral and then the son of the Klingon Worf (Michael Dorn) on Next Generation , the Bajoran scientist Dr. Mora on Deep Space Nine and the Haakonian scientist Ma’bor Jetrel on Voyager . His TV résumé also included the telefilms The Disappearance of Aimee , starring Faye Dunaway and Bette Davis, and The Billionaires Boys Club and stops on Wonder Woman , Buck Rogers in the 25th Century , Lou Grant , Falcon Crest , Knots Landing , Cagney & Lacey , Moonlighting , Murder, She Wrote , Quantum Leap , The X-Files and NYPD Blue . “Friends and colleagues remember him always present, always curious, courageous, inventive and loyal as well as brash, mouthy and very urban. He was one-of-a-kind,” his family said. Survivors include his wife, actress Deirdre Lenihan ( Needles and Pins , The Waltons ), whom he married in 1973, and their children, Daniel, a musician, and Samantha Sloyan, an actress ( The Life of Chuck , Dr. Penelope Blake on Grey’s Anatomy ). His brother, author and Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Patrick Sloyan, died in February 2019. THR

title: Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Jill Goldsmith , Dominic Patten September 21, 2026 8:11am Paramount CEO David Ellison Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC Paramount has settled an antitrust lawsuit brought by a dozen State Attorneys General led by California’s Rob Bonta, the last obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery , Deadline has confirmed. Details were scant but there will be concessions. The deal should be formally announced later this morning. Deadline hears that Paramount has agreed to some CNN guardrails, financial penalties linked to CEO David Ellison ‘s 30 movies a year commitment and some sort of separation of the studios for a period. A report in the WSJ said the company will avoid having to sell cable networks. Related Stories Legal Paramount Settlement Talks Prospects Dim For Now As Gang Of Four AGs Resist Quick Ellison Deal News Mark Ruffalo Urges AG Bonta "Do Not Cave" On Paramount Deal, Suggests Protest Outside Oakland Office: "The People Don't Want It!" The WGA’s lawsuit is included in settlement, Deadline hears. Watch on Deadline News of settlement began trickling out on Friday but four of the AGs in the group were said to be holding out. The Attorneys General of New York, Connecticut, Minnesota and Nevada came around late Sunday, we hear, after assurances from California’s Bonta that he would hold Paramount’s “feet to the fire” to ensure the company stuck to its commitments. He had said previously he preferred structural remedies like asset sales to resolve antitrust issues, rather than behavioral remedies, which require monitoring. Paramount shares are up 9% on the news. WBD gained 10% trading at about $30.50. The deal calls for Paramount to take out Warner stockholders for $31 a share. The road here has been a long one marked by a tidal wave of industry opposition, a bruising legal fight, and threats by Paramount CEO David Ellison to exit Hollywood and relocate Paramount to another state. Frontrunners Texas and Tennessee will not, it turns out, be hosting a major film and TV studio. The AGs filed their antitrust lawsuit in July, a month after the U.S. Department of Justice approved the merger, and the judge in the case set a March trial date. The two sides were scheduled to meet at a court-ordered settlement conference in mid-October but Paramount was very eager to reach a deal before Oct. 1, the start of a $7 million-a-day (25 cents per share per quarter) payout the company would owe Warner if the deal had not closed. Called a ticking fee, it’s a rarely used sweetener in M&A that Par employed to convince WBD’s board of directors to accept its offer, and that might have cost it close to $2 billion. Bonta had asked for structural remedies that were hard for Ellison to accept. But he and his team came to the table recently with ideas and things began to move . Deal In Flux Paramount announced in February it had entered into a definitive agreement to acquire WBD for $31 a share in a deal that valued WBD at $81 billion in equity value and $110 billion in enterprise value. Paramount said the combination would yield over $6 billion in synergies. The transaction was funded by $47 billion in equity and $54 billion in debt syndicated out by a consortium of banks and institutions. Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, David’s father, personally guaranteed the bulk of the equity portion. The merger moved from the DOJ through approvals by the EU, the U.K. and other territories. David Ellison continued to anticipate a close in the third quarter of 2026. But the AGs lawsuit stopped things cold. It called out alleged antitrust violations in three markets – cable programming, wide release films, and blockbuster films and won a temporary restraining order early on. Paramount agreed not to close the deal while the case was in play. The WGA also sued to block the merger, with its case running alongside the States. A public relations battle commenced with Paramount insisting the combination would revitalize the entertainment sector. A wide range of industry players disagreed, predicting massive job losses, especially given combined company’s projected $80 billion debt load. But pressure had also ratcheted up on Bonta to settle as Paramount continued to threaten a Hollywood exit and the risk of two major players in limbo through the spring posed its own risks. The Chase Ellison, 43, has amassed a media empire in record time. He launched his aggressive pursuit of WBD shortly after his Skydance Media closed an $8 billion acquisition of Paramount, buying Shari Redstone’s controlling stake in another twisty chase. He started with an escalating series of hostile bids for WBD that were rejected by its board and CEO David Zaslav, but did push Warner to formally put itself up for sale. Several other suitors stepped up. In December of 2025, Warner announced a deal to sell its studio and streaming assets to Netflix. Undeterred, Ellison continued to sweeten the terms of his offer. Ultimately, WBD ditched Netflix and in favor of a richer Paramount deal for the entire company. The giant streamer declined to counter, instead walking away with a $2.8 billion breakup fee. Larry Ellison has been a friend and was major donor to Donald Trump’s presidential campaign. He was also the biggest investor in Skydance. To secure FCC approval for the Paramount deal, the David Ellison company pledged to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs and establish a CBS News ombudsman position to review bias complaints. He installed Barry Weiss, the polarizing founder of website The Free Press, to run CBS News, all of which sparked fears of similar shakeup at CNN if the deal went through. The Paramount-AG settlement follows one final approval, from the Federal Communications Commission, On Sept. 17. The agency waived a Congressionally mandated 25% cap on foreign broadcast ownership to allow a trio of Middle East sovereign wealth funds, from Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, to own 49.5% of the merged company. They stepped in as investors with a backstop by Larry Ellison. Paramount said the funds will hold non-voting stock and have no say in governance, operating or content decisions. title: There’s a Deal, Now It’s All About the Details. Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Fight
full_text: Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Alex Weprin , Winston Cho September 21, 2026 8:03am Paramount CEO David Ellison and 12 states led by California AG Rob Bonta have agreed to terms. Getty Images Logo text They have a deal. After days of marathon negotiations, Paramount Skydance and the state attorneys general have settled the blockbuster antitrust lawsuit over the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, The Hollywood Reporter has confirmed. The agreement is expected to be announced later Monday (on Yom Kippur, no less). But it also clears Paramount to close the deal, which had a so-called $7 million-per-day ticking fee set to begin Oct. 1. The settlement allows the studio to avoid paying those costs assuming it can close in the next 10 days or so. The agreement comes after months of what has been a bitter and public back and forth, with threats by Paramount to leave the state of California (Texas and Tennessee both courted the company), accusations of antisemitism levied at some critics of the deal and a political undercurrent running just beneath the surface of the whole thing, given the Ellison family’s relationship to President Donald Trump, Rob Bonta’s own political ambitions and the hyper-politicized nature of dealmaking today. The state attorneys general, led by California’s Bonta had sued to block the deal, alleging that the merger would give the combined Paramount-Warners too much control over basic cable TV and the theatrical film business. The Writers Guild of America later joined the fray, with a lawsuit that argued the merger would suppress wages and worsen working conditions for writers by creating a single mega-buyer of film and television programming. Earlier this year, consumers had also filed a complaint challenging the purchase. Ellison, for his part, promised to release a minimum of 30 films per year theatrically, though many in the industry remain skeptical about how long the company can sustain that level of production. Bonta had maintained he’ll only accept structural remedies, which typically involve companies selling off parts of the combined business. It’s believed a sticking point for the states in any settlement involved Paramount operating the two studios as independent businesses and selling off parts of its cable business. For Ellison, parting ways with CNN was a no-go. Still, the specifics of a deal are still TBA, including any potential divestitures. The legal and public message jockeying in the court battle was contentious. Leading up to the deal, Paramount had said it would leave California if an agreement wasn’t struck by Oct. 1, when the so-called ticking fee starts accruing, regardless of the outcome of the lawsuits — a move Bonta had called “blackmail.” This came after the studio came to terms with Bonta and the WGA in a joint agreement to hold off on consummating the merger until a trial had determined whether it violated antitrust laws, though it was scheduled for next year. Across the litigation, Paramount had been rankled that the government and dozens of foreign regulators cleared the purchase. In June, the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division found that the acquisition would actually increase competition across media and entertainment. The decision cleared the way for Paramount to become among the largest theatrical distributors in the country and own a top five streamer by subscriber count, until the deal was challenged by the states. Notably, the green light didn’t require any divestitures, behavioral remedies or concessions. Paramount has framed the merger as one that will boost competition, arguing it’s necessary to compete against tech giants like Netflix, Amazon and Apple. Hollywood will soon see whether that’s true. THR

title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay Are Standouts in a Jane Austen Redo That’s Fine if Not Strictly Necessary
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 8:00am Esmé Creed-Miles (left) and Daisy Edgar-Jones in 'Sense and Sensibility.' Courtesy of Focus Features Pity any director who undertakes to remake a beloved literary property previously seen on screen in what is widely regarded as an unimprovable adaptation. That’s the daunting task faced by Georgia Oakley, who landed on the map with her assured 2022 debut feature, the politically personal queer character study Blue Jean . But the director’s take on Sense and Sensibility seldom steps out from the long shadow of Ang Lee’s enchanting 1995 retelling of the Jane Austen classic, scripted by Emma Thompson with endless amounts of verve, wit, emotional perspicacity and exquisite romantic yearning. Related Stories Movies Inde Navarrette: I Didn't "Want to Make Any Friends" During 'Obsession' Shoot to Focus on Film Movies Why 'Sense and Sensibility' Star George MacKay Still Hasn't Watched Ang Lee's Oscar-Winning Classic No disrespect to Oakley’s cast, all of whom are more than capable actors, but in almost every familiar beat of the story I found myself thinking back fondly to the actors who filled those roles for Lee — chief among them Thompson, Kate Winslet, Hugh Grant, Alan Rickman, Gemma Jones and the priceless Elizabeth Spriggs. I get it that this is intended as a fresh spin on Austen’s 1811 Regency romance, aimed at a new generation of movie lovers who have no great attachment to earlier versions. But for those of us who adore the 1995 film, unfavorable comparisons seem inevitable. Sense and Sensibility The Bottom Line Glum and glummer. Release date : Friday, Oct. 16 Cast : Daisy Edgar Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw, Stacy Martin, Tom Brooke, Turlough Convery, Chloe Pirrie, Eliot Sumner, Bethany Slater, Ceara Coveney Director : Georgia Oakley Screenwriter : Diana Reid, based on the novel by Jane Austen Rated PG, 2 hours 11 minutes One subtle shift in first-time screenwriter Diana Reid’s adaptation is the firmer centering of the quarrelsome but inextricably bonded older Dashwood sisters, Elinor ( Daisy Edgar-Jones ) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles). Of course this was always the case in Austen’s novel, right down to the way the title reflects the two sisters’ contrasting characters, with Elinor’s rationality and restraint representing “sense” and Marianne’s unguarded passion and unbridled emotionality signaling “sensibility.” Theirs is the paramount love story here, which works well in some ways but less so in others, somehow diminishing the stakes of their respective longing for Edward Ferrars ( George MacKay ) and Willoughby ( Frank Dillane ). Part of the brilliance of Thompson’s screenplay for the 1995 adaptation is that it foregrounded the sisters while also making the world they inhabited and its characters equally vivid. Here, there’s too little relief from the sisters’ downbeat moods to make us care about them. Oakley and Reid lean so heavily into Elinor and Marianne’s crushing disappointments and the forces holding them back in a period of vast gender inequity, that their sorrows shove the characters’ more captivating qualities to the side. Sense and Sensibility is a book with its fair share of melancholy — starting when Elinor, Marianne, their younger sister Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach) and their mother ( Caitríona Balfe ) are forced after Mr. Dashwood’s death to vacate their Sussex home, Norland Park, due to stringent primogeniture laws. But I can’t recall another adaptation, either for film or television, that made the story so overwhelmingly morose and its protagonists such a joyless pair. Casting John (Tom Brooke), the eldest Dashwood offspring, who inherits the estate, as a spineless weasel yields little tension because it’s obvious from the minute we meet his avaricious wife Fanny (Stacy Martin) that she will talk him down on any annual stipend he proposes allocating to his stepmother and half-sisters, in compliance with his late father’s wishes. Austen’s mean-spirited vipers — Caroline Bingley and Lady Catherine de Bourgh in Pride and Prejudice and Mrs. Elton in Emma , as well as Fanny — are as memorable as her heroines. Martin plays Fanny with the right brittle calculation, but she’s a standard-issue rich bitch. I missed the outrageous malice of the character in Lee’s version, hilariously evil in Queen of Mean Harriet Walter’s delicious turn. Humor is often a casualty here, even in the book’s most dependable source, wealthy widow Mrs. Jennings, the mother-in-law of a distant cousin of the Dashwoods, who offers them a cottage on his estate in Devonshire. Sublime English character actress Spriggs made this raucous, gossipy matchmaker a spark plug who brought fresh fizz to Lee’s film every time she appeared, as did a marvelous Imelda Staunton as her complete twit of a daughter, Charlotte. Fiona Shaw ’s work here as Mrs. J is colorless by comparison, loud and abrasive and so unable to read the room that we never get much sense of the kindness and generosity beneath the character’s overbearing manner. She just seems to require an audience. Other characters blend into the wallpaper, among them Mrs. Dashwood, wasting the considerable talents of Balfe (so wrenching as the unhappy mother in Andrew Haigh’s upcoming A Long Winter ); and Lucy Steele (Ceara Coveney), whose confidences are a form of torture for Elinor though here she’s barely around long enough to make an impression. That leaves the men, who fare well enough. Playing Edward as the courtly and compassionate polar-opposite of his awful sister Fanny, MacKay brings a gentle diffidence that syncs beautifully with Edgar-Jones’ delicate reserve. Their climactic scenes near the end, once all the obstacles have been removed, are lovely — and not just because Austen’s prose in their outcome is so indestructible. Dillane, superb in Harris Dickinson’s Urchin , has presence but is somewhat shortchanged by the script’s one-dimensional grasp of Willoughby, the dashing romantic hero revealed to be an opportunistic cad who breaks Marianne’s heart. And as the self-abnegating Colonel Brandon, Norwegian actor Herbert Nordrum (one point of the triangle in The Worst Person in the World ) is touching as he takes several steps back when he sees that Marianne’s affections lie elsewhere, then steps forward with heroic devotion when her health is in grave danger. Nordrum didn’t quite rip out my heart the way Rickman did 31 years ago, but his watchful intensity gives him one of the most moving character arcs. The performance likely to have the most fervent admirers in Creed-Miles’ as Marianne, the reckless romantic who lets her heart lead her, with devastating results. Oakley and costume designer Grace Snell break from the traditional pristine elegance in period films set in this era, making Marianne a free-spirited child of nature whose dresses and hair look consistently bedraggled, starting when she is first seen lying in long grass in the opening scene. The director certainly gets a lot of raw feeling out of the actress, but should the character really seem almost feral? The emphasis on naturalism perhaps removes some of the emotional barriers for young contemporary audiences, but it also gives the movie a low-energy feel and a drab look, with flat light and a dreary color palette. Historical sticklers will roll their eyes at all the free-flowing tresses in place of tidy updos, though the element that made me groan the most was the ball scenes. Does every post- Bridgerton period piece now have to mix traditional dance with expressively stylized modern touches? That kind of flourish has become as much a cliché as the buttoned-up starchiness of old-school costume dramas, especially when it’s as inorganic as it is here. The women just appear to have gotten lost on their way to quadrille practice and stumbled into a Pina Bausch class. Still, I suppose we should at least be grateful that Oakley for the most part held back from the gimmicky Emerald Fennell approach . Full credits Release date: Friday, Oct. 16 Production companies: Working Title, in association with November Pictures Distribution: Focus Features Cast: Daisy Edgar Jones, Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe, Bodhi Rae Breathnach, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, Fiona Shaw, Stacy Martin, Tom Brooke, Turlough Convery, Chloe Pirrie, Eliot Sumner, Bethany Slater, Ceara Coveney Director: Georgia Oakley Screenwriter: Diana Reid, based on the novel by Jane Austen Producers: Tim Bevan, Eric Fellner, India Flint, Jo Wallett Executive producers: Thea Paulett, Angela Moneke Director of photography: Arnaud Potier Production designer: Francesca Di Mottola Costume designer: Grace Snell Music: Roger Goula Editor: Izabella Curry Casting: Kharmel Cochrane Rated PG, 2 hours 11 minutes THR

title: ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic
full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic The British director’s follow-up to her BAFTA-winning “Blue Jean” brings Daisy Edgar-Jones, George MacKay, Esmé Creed-Miles, and a scene-stealing Frank Dillane together in a romantically earthy 18th-century England. By Beatrice Loayza Plus Icon Beatrice Loayza Latest ‘Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie’ Review: Alex Gibney Profiles the Controversial Author During His Harrowing Hospitalization 3 days ago ‘Hombre al Agua’ Review: Gael García Bernal Directs and Stars in a Sputtering, Screwball-y Dramedy About One Man’s Identity Crisis 1 week ago ‘A Good Little Soldier’ Review: Alba Rohrwacher Goes Corporate Drone in Stéphane Brizé’s Lukewarm Workplace Drama 2 weeks ago See All Screenshot courtesy YouTube/Focus Features It’s been over 30 years since Ang Lee’s “ Sense and Sensibility ” became (for this critic, as for many) the Platonic ideal of the Jane Austen adaptation. Lush but controlled, dryly funny (thanks to Emma Thompson’s Oscar-winning script) in that chatty, cheeky, keenly perceptive Austen way, Lee’s classic also boasted a formidable cast to unleash a floodgate of big, ugly-cry-inducing emotions by its finale. All of which is to say that Georgia Oakley had a tough act to follow in taking on the beloved tale of two sisters navigating matters of the heart in two vastly different ways. Though slightly muted (in both feeling and color palette) by comparison, Oakley’s moody, naturalistic spin on the Austen touchstone is a solid undertaking. It’s also a confident, bigger-budget follow-up to her BAFTA-winning debut “Blue Jean,” a poignant Thatcher-era queer drama; that film’s restrained yet tactile intimacy translates well to a late 18th-century England of stifled desire and pastoral exuberance. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony There’s an earthy romanticism to Oakley’s vision of the times, with shots of quivering cattails, dew-spotted spiders, and floating lilypads complementing the roiling inner lives of sisters Elinor ( Daisy Edgar-Jones ) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) Dashwood. The younger Marianne is the more daring and vivacious of the two — a lightly shaky camera is on her heels as she adventures through the forest and receives news of their father’s death — and thankfully Oakley avoids the corny Mother Earth symbolism (à la “Hamnet”) that woodsy women amid sun-dappled pastures can so easily invite. The film’s natural splendor is pleasing, of course, but Oakley makes a point to show the grit and exhaustion of scaling hills and taking multi-day journeys by horse carriage — tough physical realities matched by the cruel social conventions that upend the Dashwoods’ lives. Popular on Variety Hewing close to the novel’s major plot beats, Diana Reid’s script efficiently lays out the stakes, as mother Dashwood (Caitríona Balfe) finds herself penniless and powerless against the takeover of her family’s estate by John Dashwood (Tom Brooke), her dead husband’s only male heir from his first marriage. Before she and the girls relocate to a modest seaside cottage in Devon, they suffer insults from John’s comically stingy wife Fanny (a wonderfully catty Stacy Martin) while Elinor meet-cutes with Fanny’s brother Edward ( George MacKay ), their mutual affection growing over wholesome nature walks and portrait sessions. (In a sweet reversal of the typical gendered gaze, it’s Elinor who draws Edward.) Sadly, Edward is too spineless and, er, sensible to follow his heart and lets a confused Elinor slip away when her family finally retreats to their new isolated home, courtesy of the kindly but coarse Mrs. Jennings (Fiona Shaw). For her part, the blunt and free-spirited Marianne finds her match in the dashing Willoughby ( Frank Dillane , the face of Harris Dickinson’s “Urchin”), brushing off the endearingly awkward advances of Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum, from “The Worst Person in the World,” speaking in a placid baritone). In Devon, Marianne and Willoughby enjoy a rustic romance of piano dueting and cliffside snuggling, and though he makes quite the statement in giving her a white steed, he never commits before heading back to London and remaining there for the foreseeable future. London is where Edward is, too, so when Mrs. Jennings plans a trip to the capital, Marianne and Elinor eagerly tag along. The girls’ weathered white gowns and tousled, stallionesque manes confer a cottage-core modernity that’s set in contrast to the gilded interiors and tightly-wound updos of their London acquaintances. Between the two sisters, Elinor’s prudence and Marianne’s joie de vivre are charted out via Holly Blakey’s enchanting choreography: In the country, Marianne and Willoughby partake in a riotous, rollicking folk dance, while Elinor and Edward cross paths at a buzzy London ball where they dance a comparably restrained, yet slinky, sensual waltz. Oakley’s beautifully textured worldbuilding — of soft, candlelit interiors; hunted game hanging on wall hooks; and so very many neat dogs (pugs, sheepdogs, mastiffs, whippets!) — is paired with a quivering psychological realism. Low-angle close-ups betray the fragility of Elinor’s self-composure when Edward tells her that he is engaged to another woman; and Marianne is a jittery bundle of broken idealism when she finds Willoughby arm-in-arm with a wealthy fiancé. These lovers’ quarrels unfold with a touching sincerity to Roger Goula’s wistful score, though Oakley’s more grounded drama also feels oddly safe, with a seriousness of tone that strips away some of the wit and comedy that makes Austen’s work, well, Austenesque. And though players like Edgar-Jones and MacKay make for perfectly tender lovebirds, they don’t exactly breathe new life into their characters. This might be the difference between being a gifted actor and a real star, which Lee’s “Sense and Sensibility” had across the board. Creed-Miles’ sharp-tongued, twinkle-eyed Marianne comes close to that inexplicable magnetism, though the script, which makes her sound like a broken record with the number of times she goes on about passion and passionate men, renders her a tad clichéd. In terms of casting, what Oakley’s “Sense and Sensibility” does confirm is that Dillane’s recent breakthrough was no fluke. His Willoughby is a slouching, smug-faced scoundrel — a rake all his own, and perhaps the only major presence in the film that brings an unstudied lightness and humor to this world of breath-held decorum. ‘Sense and Sensibility’ Review: Georgia Oakley Puts a Moody, Naturalistic Spin on the Jane Austen Classic Reviewed at Universal Screening Room, New York City, Sept. 18, 2026. full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Reza Rahadian, Dian Sastrowardoyo Starrer ‘Descendants of the Sun’ Heads to Busan Market as Barunson E&A Launches Sales 31 minutes ago ‘A Teacher’s Gift’ Lands U.K. Distribution Deal With Peccadillo Pictures (EXCLUSIVE) 6 hours ago Bestselling Japanese Novelist Maha Harada Says ‘If This Is a Dream, I Hope I Never Wake Up’ About Her San Sebastian – and Busan – Bound Directing Debut ‘In My Father’s Room’ 6 hours ago See All Barunson E&A Barunson E&A will launch international sales for “ Descendants of the Sun ,” a big-screen version of the landmark Korean series that first aired in 2016, at the Asian Contents & Film Market in Busan, running Oct. 10-13. The Seoul-based company, known for producing Bong Joon Ho’s Academy Award winner “Parasite,” is making the film alongside Dapur Film, Tobali Putra Productions, NEWKO and Barunson C&C, its own subsidiary production arm. NEW (Next Entertainment World), owner of the original intellectual property, has come on board as a co-production company. Part One is aiming for an Indonesian theatrical bow by mid-2027. Popular on Variety The adaptation arrives at the original series’ 10th anniversary, a show many credit with helping bring K-drama to global audiences. The original drew a 38.8% rating in its home market, marked the first instance of a Korean drama airing simultaneously in China, where iQIYI logged upward of two billion streams, and eventually found distribution in more than 30 territories, among them the U.S., the U.K., France, Germany, Japan and Russia. The series was similarly popular in Indonesia a decade ago, fueling anticipation for the new version before any footage had surfaced. The Indonesian film relocates the central romance to a setting and cultural backdrop specific to Indonesia while retaining what the studio describes as the emotional core of the original. Hanung Bramantyo, one of Indonesia’s leading box office directors, helms the project. He previously directed “Miracle in Cell No. 7,” an Indonesian version of the identically titled Korean film that ranks as the country’s eighth-highest-grossing domestic release. Reza Rahadian and Dian Sastrowardoyo lead the cast. Rahadian’s credits include “Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash,” which won the Golden Leopard at Locarno, and Sastrowardoyo has appeared in Netflix’s “Cigarette Girl” as well as “The Fox King,” a Toronto Film Festival premiere. “Ten years on, ‘Descendants of the Sun’ is still one of the titles people point to when they talk about the start of the K-drama wave,” said Barunson E&A CEO Yoonhee Choi. “We see the strength of the Korean IP as a starting point, not an endpoint. This adaptation places that globally recognized story under a different sun, in an Indonesian landscape with a local sensibility all its own. It retains the familiarity of a story audiences already know and love, while opening it to a new context and, we believe, audiences beyond Indonesia.” “As the producer behind the original series, I deeply admire how the director has honored its spirit while creating a truly Indonesian story that I believe will translate just as powerfully wherever it’s seen,” added Woosik Seo, CEO of Barunson C&C and an executive producer on the film. “Descendants of the Sun” heads an ACFM slate for Barunson E&A that also includes “Satan’s Slaves: Origin,” a prequel to Joko Anwar’s horror franchise, whose first two entries are among Indonesia’s highest-earning local films; “Stoneborn,” an occult mystery from the “Exhuma” creative team starring Jongseo Jeon of Cannes title “Burning” and Sul Kyung-gu of Venice title “Possible Love”; and “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng,” a comedy debuting at the Busan International Film Festival ahead of an Oct. 28 theatrical release. ‘The Odyssey’ and ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Power $239 Million U.K., Ireland July Box Office Korea Box Office: Local Comedy Remake ‘The Intern’ Leads Weekend Admissions as ‘The Odyssey’ Retains Revenue Crown Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Eclipses ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Continues Dominance ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Continue Tussle Atop U.K., Ireland Box Office John Carpenter, Colman Domingo and Charlize Theron to Be Honored at Academy Museum Gala Loading comments... title: Carly Rae Jepsen on How Marriage, Motherhood and the Joy of Pop Music Fueled Her Ambitious Double Album ‘Day and Night’: ‘I Knew What Colors I Was Playing With’
full_text: Sep 21, 2026 8:00am PT Carly Rae Jepsen on How Marriage, Motherhood and the Joy of Pop Music Fueled Her Ambitious Double Album ‘Day and Night’: ‘I Knew What Colors I Was Playing With’ By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Jhené Aiko Scores First No. 1 on Albums Chart With ‘Westside Whimsy’ 20 hours ago Chad Gilbert, New Found Glory Guitarist and Backing Vocalist, Dies at 45 20 hours ago Jay-Z Revisits the Ghosts of Lyrics Past in the Illuminating (and Possibly Too Thorough) ‘Jay-Z in 8’: TV Review 3 days ago See All Courtesy of Mikayla LoBasso It sounds like an obvious approach, but Carly Rae Jepsen began working on her new double album “Day and Night” with a simple ethos: make the type of music she would want to listen to. “Like, what do I have to offer to the musical landscape right now?” the 40-year-old tells Variety over Zoom, just weeks before her sixth album released this past Friday. “And that began with how I always begin every project, which is, what am I attracted to? What music am I listening to that I love?” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony As evidenced by the album’s two-dozen tracks, split evenly between Laurel Canyon coffee pop and synth-glittered bops, “Day and Night” is an amalgamation of self-professed influences — a “mixed bag of chips,” she says — inspired by artists and styles spanning Blossom Dearie and Minnie Ripperton to ABBA and house music. The “Day” section of the album is decidedly folksy, packed with organic instrumentation across tracks like acoustic ballad “Wild Child” and shimmying “After All,” while “Night” slips into something a bit more mischievous on the smoky “Amalfi Coast” and effervescent “Don’t Leave Me on the Dance Floor.” Popular on Variety For anyone who’s followed her since her explosion into mainstream pop with 2012’s “Call Me Maybe,” it’s clear that Jepsen is a creature of creation, consistently amassing songs until they start to take shape as a project. (She famously recorded 250 songs for her seminal sophomore album “Emotion,” which she recently celebrated with a 10th anniversary show at Los Angeles’ Troubadour.) With “Day and Night,” Jepsen had been working on material and was a quarter of the way through the process when she presented her work to her guitarist, Tavish Crowe, who realized that she was making music in two distinct lanes. “He said, ‘What if it’s like a house party, and as a thought experiment, we make this the upstairs and the downstairs?'” she recalls. “So we started doing that for fun. And then ‘Day and Night’ was born when I was just driving in my car here in LA. I loved its simplicity. It perfectly described this organic kind of dreamy thing, and then the nighttime, you immediately feel things get heightened and a little darker and more experimental. So then I would show up with sessions with a bit more intention and it became really fun because I knew what colors I was playing with.” “Day and Night” is also a diary, of sorts, as Jepsen began to fall in love with her now-husband Cole Marsden Greif-Neill, known to the music world as Cole M.G.N., whose credits include Beck, Wallows and Christine and the Queens. They had previously worked together on “So Right,” included on her 2023 album “The Loveliest Time,” and on “Day and Night,” he contributes to a handful of tracks — some of which are directly inspired by their burgeoning romance. Throughout the record, Jepsen sings of surrendering to this newfound love, of basking in the resplendence and joy that it brings. Mainly, she says, there’s an element of “how shocked I am that this is all happening.” She explains that she’s always thought of herself as an artistic observer of life, as opposed to a participant, and that in the past, she’d written about relationships that may have been doomed because she loved “an impossible situation.” “I think that the idea of really engaging, saying yes to the whole thing — a baby, a child, a family, a forever — that felt like big stuff,” she says. “So it wasn’t until I really met Cole that I — and probably even before I met Cole — that I had done some of my own personal work to get to a place where I was ready to meet a man like Cole, where I was like, okay, this is wild. I want all the things. And even the first time I might have even admitted that to myself was when I was writing ‘After All,’ which is how I decided to open the album so boldly. Like, alright, here we go!” Jepsen lights up when talking about the very first day she met Greif-Neill, when they ended up in the studio to write “Day and Night” cut “No Labels, I Love You.” “I was driving home from that session and I thought, cute guy, but [only] in there. Not gonna touch that hot stuff. And you know, don’t kiss the producer. Rule number one,” she says with a laugh. She pulled to a stop sign and saw he had texted her with questions about the song’s second verse and decided to save his number under a combination of his name and the track they had just worked on. “I put ‘Cole I Love You’ in my phone. Lo and behold, five years later, we’re married with a baby, and I’m like, oh. Well, that worked out. He’s still saved as ‘Cole I Love You’ because of that day.” Shortly after marrying in October 2025, Jepsen and Greif-Neill welcomed their first child in March amid the completion of “Day and Night.” She had been prepping for the baby’s arrival while balancing the demands of being a pop star — at the “Emotion” anniversary show in August 2025, she says she was four months pregnant and wore a dress with “distracting lines” in hopes of making it an “optical illusion” — and is gradually learning how to delineate between family and career. “I’m more of a planner than I’ve ever been before,” she says. “A big part of getting ready for this double album and mixing it and putting the art together and even preparing like what videos were shot when was all around the idea of like, baby’s on the way. It was like a different meaning for the word deadline… And there was a conversation of, am I doing this before the baby comes or after the baby comes? It was like, before, because after the baby comes, I’m gonna be focused. So it’s changed that in a really wild way that I didn’t expect. It was so obvious what the priority was, which was building a career around a life, not the other way around.” That includes making time for the Broadway adaptation of the 1999 rom-com “10 Things I Hate About You,” set for previews in August 2027. Lena Dunham is adapting the musical’s book with Jessica Huang, while Jepsen is writing the music and lyrics with Ethan Gruska, whose credits include Ryan Beatty, Fiona Apple and Phoebe Bridgers. “We wanted to handle with care, but not trepidation,” she says of the musical. “We wanted to feel emboldened to think about what would cause these characters to feel like words are not enough and they need to break into the song. So we began with playlists for each character. Bianca had like her ’90s playlist. And it became really fun to sort of think about, you know, what the message of our show is.” Jepsen stops short of giving too much away: When asked about how she plans to handle the iconic scene where Heath Ledger’s character sings Frankie Valli’s “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You,” she demurs. “That one you’re gonna have to come and see. I know, disappointing answer, but I gotta leave some for the show.” For now, Jepsen is enjoying the spoils of motherhood as she releases one of her most ambitious projects to date. In the past, she’s complemented her studio albums by releasing full companion records of B-sides, something she’s not entirely counting out for “Day and Night. “In a very elusive way, in a very non-sexy way, I’ll say I consider myself sort of like a chipmunk,” she jokes. “I like to store my ideas in my cheeks, save them for later. Who knows.” But, as always, she’s looking for the next spark of inspiration. “A big part of my nature is to be in constant creation. I like to be making things. I don’t find it tiring,” she says. “It fuels and excites me. One of my greatest joys, even when I’m on the road is to pull up with Tavish and be like, hey, like late night tonight, let’s go to like your hotel or my hotel and we’ll get the office space and pull up some sound and just jam. That’s going to be different with a baby, but we’re going to figure out how to make that happen and fit it in between the cracks.” ‘The Odyssey’ Becomes Universal’s Highest-Grossing Film of All Time Korea Box Office: ‘The Odyssey’ Bests ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Box Office: ‘Practical Magic 2’ Conjures Up $13 Million on Friday as ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Nears All-Time Domestic Box Office Record ‘The Odyssey’ Leaked on X: High-Quality Bootleg Seen by Millions in Hours Before Takedown ‘The Odyssey’ Sets 20,000 Screen China Release, Including Near-Total Imax Commitment (EXCLUSIVE) China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Continues Dominance Loading comments... title: Melissa McCarthy on Getting Serious for ‘JonBenét Ramsey,’ the Psychiatrist on Set and Hollywood’s ‘Bulls—’ Excuse for Why Comedies Don’t Work Anymore
full_text: Ramona Rosales for Variety Melissa McCarthy , one of the most gifted comic actors working today, will soon be starring in a tragedy. In “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” — premiering on Netflix on Dec. 10 — McCarthy plays Patsy Ramsey, the mother of 6-year-old JonBenét, who was killed in the Ramseys’ Boulder, Colorado, home on Christmas night in 1996. Because JonBenét had won several child beauty pageants, images of her in makeup and garish costumes created a spectacle around the case (which is still unsolved), and around the Ramseys. JonBenét’s father, John; her mother, and even her 9-year-old brother, Burke, all became suspects in her murder, and the series examines the fallout from her death. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension Ramona Rosales for Variety Because of the O.J. Simpson trial in 1995, true crime had become a national obsession, and with JonBenét’s murder, newsmagazines, talk shows and tabloids had a field day, inciting the public to rabidity: Today, McCarthy remembers being part of the “feeding frenzy” herself. Clive Owen, who plays John, says McCarthy’s involvement as both an actor and executive producer was a “big part” of the reason he agreed to take the role. “Yes, she’s a brilliant comedic actress, but she’s just a brilliant actress ,” Owen says. Popular on Variety “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” from showrunner Richard LaGravenese (and made without the family’s involvement), was an emotionally wrenching endeavor, and McCarthy and Owen formed a bond. “We have become friends,” he says. “Because it was such a difficult project, just having her alongside as an ally was really, really important. And honestly, after doing this project with her — she can do anything.” And she has. After playing chef Sookie St. James in the beloved dramedy “Gilmore Girls” from 2000 to 2007, McCarthy broke out in film in 2011’s Paul Feig-directed blockbuster “Bridesmaids” as the crude yet earnest Megan. The scene-stealing role brought her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination, a rarity for comedy — especially given that in the film’s famously gruesome food poisoning set-piece, Megan uses a sink as a toilet. McCarthy was shocked when she learned of her nomination, saying to her husband, director Ben Falcone, “I don’t think that’s true,” when he told her. (McCarthy was nominated for an Oscar a second time, for her fearless lead performance in Marielle Heller’s 2018 “Can You Ever Forgive Me?”) Over her career, McCarthy has starred in hit comedies such as Feig’s “The Heat” and “Spy” and Falcone’s “Tammy” and “The Boss” — and as the villainous Ursula in Disney’s 2023 live-action version of “The Little Mermaid.” But with “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” she returns to her earliest training in New York City, when she spent two years studying the Sanford Meisner method of acting. Back then, McCarthy was “carrying folding chairs up to a rehearsal space to do a show and just making enough money to hopefully pay for the space that night.” Despite the different scale of audience, the same passion and community spirit went into “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” McCarthy says in her first interview about the series, with the cast and crew putting in “hardworking days” while suffering through “hard moments.” Wanting to do right by Patsy, who died of ovarian cancer in 2006, McCarthy found people who knew her. “And they were like, ‘Those kids were in jeans riding their bikes. JonBenét wasn’t out in a pageant dress in her front yard.’” Playing Patsy Ramsey is such a heavy thing — what went into your decision to do it? I said, “Oh, no. I have no interest in that.” I didn’t think it was any of my business to do, I guess? But I spent a lot of years not working, and somebody took the time to ask me — I should take the time to look into it. The more I started to, I was really floored by the lack of humanity that had been shown to that family. In 1996, I was 26, and I have a very vivid memory of standing in a grocery store and looking at a tabloid and thinking, “How could you dress a little girl like that?” Because that’s what we were being told. I remember being obsessed. I had never put it together that I was a part of [judging them]. I went willingly. And that’s on me. I just thought if it can make some people realize, “Oh, God. I was part of that — I did that,” it gives us a little of our humanity back. And the hope is not to dredge it up for that poor family again. This might sound nuts: I’m very fond of Patsy. I have so much compassion for them, what they went through, and go through currently. That’s a bizarre thing to have a child’s trauma be like Wimbledon. It was a turning point, being able to watch something like that as sport. And even when I finally decided to do this, everybody said their theory [about the case] as if it was true. People in your life, you mean? People in my life! Very smart people, very open-minded people. I was like, “What is that based on?” Because I’ve now read every police report, every coroner’s report. So we’re still doing that. I said, “You got caught up in the riptide.” I hope with my whole heart that this — I don’t know if “helps” is the right word. Clive Owen and Melissa McCarthy Courtesy of Chris Large/Paramount+ Does the show have a point of view about what happened? This is not a whodunit. It’s not like, “Ooh, there’s a big reveal!” This is a character study of everyone who was caught in the undertow, and a look at all of us — as a civilization, really. Seeing that happen to a child I think breaks everybody. We do show all these different theories. They were all real working theories. Showing the chaos of it is something that we’ve not seen. It’s a new telling of it, because you’re like, “My God, is this really what was happening?” For your performance’s sake, did you decide what you thought happened? Yes. Just my personal feeling. My heart says no one in the family could have done that. I don’t have the ability, or probably the right, to say that, but that’s what my gut says. Which I probably am not supposed to say. But shooting that, I had to pick. I had to have that for myself, if nothing else. It’s such a heartbreaking and very physical performance as Patsy. In the two episodes I’ve seen, you’re crying so much. What was that like? It’s tricky. Luckily, I loved who I was working with. I’d never worked with Clive before — I can’t say enough good stuff about him. What a joy of a human. Everybody in the cast, every single person, they’re fantastic. It just felt elevated. And I felt like everybody knew that we had to do right by the story and not just try to do something that’s going to get a lot of views. That set was so serious, and some of those days were so hard. We had a psychologist on set at all times. You did? And it was needed sometimes, especially during some of the really intense scenes. It would take people down, and they’d just need a minute. I felt obligated to stand up for her, which — maybe it’s none of my damn business, but I feel protective of her. It makes you get up and go to work every day and try to give it your all. This show was filmed in Calgary, far from your home with Ben and your two teenage daughters. After the workday, were you taking Patsy with you? I had rather weird sleeping hours. It would depend on what the next day held, but I called my kids, for sure, and my husband, and made sure throughout the day I talked to them and checked in on days when I could. Some days I couldn’t. I didn’t want them to see me in that state. Sleep wasn’t always great when that’s what was in my head. But I was like, “Well, I bet she wasn’t sleeping great either. So get up! Get up.” As you prepare for the show to come out, what have you been thinking about? I think about the one thing I can’t control, which is how people will receive it. And, of course, you think about the family. My intentions don’t mean anything — their feelings are their feelings, and all I can do is hope that I did right by them and by Patsy. The only people that really get a vote are them. Patsy Ramsey died in 2006. But would you ever be interested in talking to John or Burke Ramsey? I would. Again, I don’t know if I’m supposed to say this: I’ve written John many letters that I haven’t sent. I wrote before we did it. I wrote, during the thing, to him and Burke — many letters — to be like, “I’m doing my best by her. I’m really trying to show who I felt she was.” “Bridesmaids”: Melissa McCarthy, Ellie Kemper, Rose Byrne, Wendi McLendon-Covey, Maya Rudolph, Kristen Wiig Courtesy of ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection You’ve excelled at drama, and this role is as dramatic as it gets. But you came up through the Groundlings, the improv and sketch program, where you met your husband, Ben Falcone, and “Bridesmaids” screenwriters Kristen Wiig and Annie Mumolo, along with so many other people you’ve gone on to work with. How did you get involved with the Groundlings? My very first stuff in New York was stand-up. I did all the free cheap rooms where you got a minute and a half, and you worked your way up to two and a half minutes and so on. But then I didn’t like those rooms anymore — I just found them really misogynistic. There was literally a guy in every room saying, “Show me your tits.” To the point where I was like, “Is it the same guy? The same lonely guy?” He’s not going to stop. The only way to make him stop is to eviscerate him. I was like, “I’m here to try to make people laugh, and now the only way I win is if I actually embarrass you. I see I’ve done that and now you’re quiet. So now I feel terrible.” I love live performance; it’s my favorite. But that realm was not. I didn’t want a fistfight. And then I moved to L.A., and my sister sent me a little magazine story about the Groundlings. I see. I was like, “Oh, there must be amazing theater in L.A.!,” because I’d never been here when I moved here. When I was doing stand-up, I didn’t really know how to write, so a lot of it was improvised. I also had a thing of like, “You’re not a writer unless you’ve been trained to write.” I would always go up with a paper, and I would do my monologue, and Ben was the first person that leans over and he goes, “Why do you always go up with a blank page?” I was like, “What? What are you talking about?” He’s like, “You go up with a blank page, you do a monologue.” I was like, “That’s not writing.” And he’s like, “It is writing.” I was like, “No, it’s not, because I don’t know how to write.” He’s like, “You just did a whole monologue, and then you wrote down what you said.” I had such a weird, I didn’t go to college — I’m not a writer. Groundlings literally taught me to be like, “OK: You are writing, you are doing this.” What was the “Bridesmaids” experience like once the movie came out? The fact that Kristen and Annie let me come in for that truly changed my life. I thought I blew the audition because I got too weird, because I was sitting there improvising with Kristen. I got too comfortable! I said weird things! Before “Bridesmaids” was released, people were like, “The numbers are not looking good.” And I was like, “It’s not out yet.” And they’re like, “We know how to do this, and the numbers are not looking good.” And I was like, “OK, but I’m just saying I think it’s really funny and I think people are going to think it’s really funny.” Opening night, Ben and I were sitting in Paul Feig’s backyard with him and his wife, Laurie, and we’re having dinner and Paul’s like, “Oh my God. Oh my God. I think it’s working! It’s working!” Then all of a sudden he’s like, “Every theater in L.A. is full. Get in the car, get in the car, get in the car!” We went to the ArcLight, I think? We just stood in the back, and it was rolling, crazy laughter. You, Ben, Paul and Laurie? Yes. We were like, “Oh my God, it’s working! What we think is funny is funny!” It was about that group of people; it was about the characters. Just running through theaters, and Paul in his suit — and Ben and I not dressed as nicely. No one does dress as nicely as Paul Feig. No, nobody. It also felt important — a comedy about women becoming such a massive success. Yes. Which is insane, but it did. Two women wrote it; we all felt like this is what’s funny . This is what we as women write about and talk about, and we are this weird. And it wasn’t about, “My dress isn’t perfect!” even though that was part of it. This is what trying on dresses really is like — it’s a bit of a shitshow. Literally. Well-played. As soon as the movie came out, people started saying you needed to be nominated for an Oscar — which you were! But that’s so uncommon for a comedy. What was that like? Disorienting. Now I can’t remember if Octavia’s name was said first or mine. Jim Rash and Nat Faxon were nominated for “The Descendants.” Kristen and Annie were nominated for screenplay — this was, like, our weird ragtag group. And I just kept saying “Octavia’s nominated!” Ben went, “Mooch, you just got nominated.” I was like, “I know Octavia got nominated for an Oscar!” And he was like, “ You just got nominated for an Oscar.” I was like, “I don’t think that’s true.” And he’s like, “We just watched it.” Then I just balled my eyes out. Right! That was the year Octavia Spencer, also your friend since the Groundlings days, won for “The Help.” And Jim and Nat won that year. We were all just there — and we were like, “What are we all doing here? This is amazing!” But our own Academy, our own industry, doesn’t respect comedy. I don’t know when that became the thing to do — and you can call any project a comedy to get into an awards category. Anybody just gets to claim it, because no real comedies are ever going to get awarded. I’m stopped 15 times a day by somebody who says, “I desperately need you to do another comedy.” And I’m like, “We are trying. I’m trying!” And people need it, that’s for sure. “The Heat”: Sandra Bullock and Melissa McCarthy ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection Can you talk about your creative partnership with Paul Feig? Paul should be legally bound to make one comedy at least every two years. His taste level as a filmmaker, his visual aesthetic, is so good — which is important. You have to make a proper film. It has to look good. It has to have great pacing. And he’s just funny as hell. He just wants to lift other people to be as funny and as good as you can possibly be. I miss him doing comedies — for myself, but also as an audience member. We’ve made it so hard to do comedies that we have our best and our funniest people not doing what they do. Why is that? I think the narrative of comedies don’t work anymore is bullshit. I think it’s absolute bullshit. It’s a false narrative. Comedy is like music. It’s a feeling — not everybody can do the same thing. Two equally incredible musicians have totally different styles. You don’t go in and break someone’s style or what they do; you have them do the best of what they can do. I think because people can laugh at a movie, for some reason, it’s less respected. And so they think, “Well, I know what’s funny.” And I always want to be like, “You’ve never been funny to me! You’ve never said anything funny. You’ve never thought of a funny idea.” It doesn’t mean you’re not great at your job — Are we talking about the executive level now? People at all the levels are now like, “Let me tell you who to put in to make it funny…” And I’m like, “Well, those four people aren’t funny.” It’s like Feig putting in Jason Statham in “Spy.” Oh God, yes! Paul and I went out to dinner with Statham, and we were just goofing around the table, and I was like, “Stop talking about it! Just do what you’re doing — it’s so funny.” But Paul had the idea to be like, “What about Statham?” But when you take all of the artists out of it — they start to do the math of it, and that’s not comedy. They want a big premise. But most really great comedies, it’s about the people and the characters and the story, and it’s not like, “And they were both aliens at the end!” But people really think they want that hook, and it’s just not real. Then they say comedies don’t work, and I’m like, “No, bad comedies don’t work.” And I won’t take the fall for that. “Spy” Melissa McCarthy and Jason Statham ©20thCentFox/Courtesy Everett Collection To me, in a just world, “Spy” would be a franchise. We should be on the ninth “Spy”! Everyone on “Spy” was ready to re-rack immediately. There should be a new villain, new location. Why didn’t it happen? Because you’re a woman? No — well, Jesus, that probably doesn’t help, but I don’t know. It did so well. People can say that doesn’t matter. I think it does. For “Thunder Force,” we were going to roll right into another one. We were like, “It’s so fun. It did incredibly well for Netflix. We already have the idea for it.” If I write something — or Ben and I write something — and it tanks, I’ll take the fall. Which we have not had to take. We don’t make $8 billion. We don’t make those kind of movies, but, I mean, $120 million, I’m not mad at that. The studio’s not mad at that. We want to make a reasonably priced thing that makes you a good profit. For some reason, that model is no longer desirable. I can’t figure out the math of it. For the never-made “Bridesmaids 2,” I’d heard that Kristen and Annie’s idea was that was Lillian gets divorced, and there’s a divorce party. Why did that not happen? And how! That I don’t know. I know that was a hard movie to make. It was, but it was also so fun. Oh my God , it was so fun. Literally laughing on set in such a way that I am shocked that we shot stuff. Rose [Byrne] is such a wonderful, bad laugher. On the plane, her little stick arms are up, and when Ben and I are doing our weird thing, she just laughs out loud . It’s a glorious thing. She just kept putting the magazine up to hide — and it’s in the movie. So that was what shooting was like. It was like you were literally hiding because someone was always like, “Oh, I’ve dropped something,” because they’re under the table laughing. That’s just not a bad day. I don’t know. I think it’s gotten so corporate. I miss the people that work off their gut. When I think about the hellish world that we live in now, I can kind of trace it directly back to the backlash against “Ghostbusters” in 2016. [ Sighs ] What madness. It does really correlate! When people were like, “You’re ruining our childhood,” I was like, “You definitely seem like you had a terrible childhood.” It just had so many cooks in that kitchen. Katie Dippold co-wrote “Ghostbusters” with Paul Feig — for her “Widow’s Bay” triumph. Oh my God , I loved her show. I almost got nervous, like, “It’s so good. Is it not going to do well?” And I ate it up. I couldn’t get enough fast enough. Then I just started hearing person after person be like, “Have you watched this thing?” It is not shocking that Katie Dippold wrote something incredible. I’m just like, who’s the genius that backed off and let her? “Gilmore Girls”: Melissa McCarthy and Lauren Graham ©CW Network/Courtesy Everett Collection Sookie on “Gilmore Girls” was your first big role. It’s not easy to do Amy Sherman-Palladino dialogue! It’s good training, I tell you that! What was that experience like when you look back on it? It was hard! It was really hard. But to me, that was normal, because it was my first show. So I was like, “Oh, our scripts are 93 pages, and you can’t change a contraction, even if you get them that morning and it’s a 10-page oner.” And that’s just what it was. I love that she had her own style, and I love that she built that world. I love that she fought for it, because a woman running that show at that time, I think you kind of had to be like, “It’s my way or the highway.” I think she had to probably fight to keep it the way she wanted to. And I’m glad she did, because it stood the test of time. People really take ownership of that show. So huge with Gen Z. And the fact that they keep re-watching it. I’m like, “Really?” It’s so funny, my kids have not watched it. But Vivian and I were both home with the flu — this is years ago. And it came on and she was like, “That’s your show, right? That was your first show?” I was like, “You’re on the very end of that show when I’m pregnant.” I think I’d had four kids on the show. And then I finally went to Amy and I’m like, “I’m actually pregnant. You can have me have another kid again, and I’ll give you the prop for free.” And she was like, “No, I don’t think so.” So then I had to hide it! I was like, “We already have four kids. I can’t have five?” But we watched just the pilot, and Vivi, my oldest, she kept going, “What are you doing with your voice?” And I was like, “Oh, it’s youth.” She’s like, “That doesn’t sound like you at all.” I was like, “Yeah! I was youthful and I didn’t have kids yet. And now I sound like this grizzled old man.” Courtesy of The CW You did one day on the Netflix revival, “Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life.” It was fun to see everybody again. I still see Lauren [Graham] and Yanic [Truesdale]. We’ve gone on vacation with Yanic. We’re really close. I just wanted to go and see everybody. So it was really nice to do. I always wonder, will something else happen with that? I don’t know anything about it, but — Amy has done a ton, but it’s kind of her life’s work, right? When something catches like that, there’s no rhyme or reason. You have to just love it. I mean, I’m always shocked at all the “Gilmore” comments when I’m out. I’m like, “I’ve worked since then!” But it is nice. And I think we all are very aware of that, or I hope so. But when something catches like that, like “That’s my comfort show,” or, “That’s what I watch going to sleep” — what a thing to get to do something that gives people comfort like that. Totally. It’s the coziest. It’s the coziest! I felt lucky doing it, and I feel lucky to have been a part of it. Courtesy of Joyful Heart Foundation Charity Spotlight: Joyful Heart Foundation Melissa McCarthy remembers meeting Mariska Hargitay the old-fashioned way: through their assistants. Hargitay, McCarthy says, seemed like someone who “probably has her shit together” enough to make recommendations for, say, “a good water filtration system.” Their texting relationship soon blossomed into a real-life friendship, which, McCarthy says, “doesn’t always happen when you meet a new friend in your 50s.” As Hargitay puts it, “When we finally did meet in person, our hearts did a dance.” Their dynamic is a playful one. When Hargitay rolled her ankle and needed surgery in July 2021, McCarthy stood on a Burbank street holding a sign asking drivers to honk to speed up the “SVU” star’s recovery. And earlier this year, McCarthy surprised Hargitay by doing a cameo on “SVU.” (“I still don’t know how they pulled it off,” Hargitay says.) For her Power of Women charity, McCarthy is putting a spotlight on Joyful Heart Foundation, which — inspired by the subject matter of “SVU” — Hargitay began in 2004 to advocate for survivors of sexual assault, domestic violence and child abuse. While other actors might have just said, “This is what I do for a living,” McCarthy says, Hargitay instead embraced it as a responsibility. “Her power is through kindness and consideration and a moral compass.” For Hargitay’s part, she says of McCarthy, “It’s a gift to find someone who’s willing to roll up their sleeves and help bring change.” Styling: Katja Cahill; Stylist assistants: Aliya Iahijani, Tracey Moore; Tailor: Daniela Kurrle; Makeup: Afton Williams; Hair: Mark Townsend/Forward Artists; Dress: L’Academie, Hat: Sadie James, Cape: Viviano; Earrings: KerenWolf, Spectrum Jewels , and Mindi Mond New York; Rings: On Aura Tout Vu, Spectrum Jewels, Le Vian Jewelry and Zales;Necklaces: Zales and Sterling Forever; Bracelets: Zales and Sterling Forever Loading comments... title: ‘Parasite’ Producer Barunson E&A Launches Sales On Indonesian Adaptation Of ‘Descendants Of The Sun’
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Dekanalog Takes North American Rights To Tan Siyou’s Festival Hit ‘Amoeba’ Pingyao Film Festival Unveils 10th Edition Line-up; ‘Spring In A Small Town’ Set As Opening Film CJ ENM Sells ‘Hotel Del Luna’, ‘Signal’ & Other Hit K-Dramas To CME Slovakia & Czech Channels View All September 21, 2026 8:00am Descendants Of The Sun Dapur Film Seoul-based studio Barunson E&A, which has credits including Bong Joon Ho’s Oscar winner Parasite , is launching international sales on the Indonesian adaptation of landmark Korean drama Descendants Of The Sun at the upcoming Asian Contents & Film Market ( ACFM ) in Busan. Currently in post-production, the two-part feature film adaptation of the 2016 Korean series is headlined by two of Indonesia’s biggest stars, Reza Rahadian ( Vengeance Is Mine, All Others Pay Cash ) and Dian Sastrowardoyo ( Cigarette Girl ). The film is produced by Dapur Film, Tobali Putra Productions, Newko and Barunson C&C, a subsidiary production company of Barunson E&A, with N.E.W. (Next Entertainment World), which holds the original IP rights, joining the project as co-producer. Production has wrapped on the two parts of the film, with part one targeting a theatrical release in Indonesia in the first half of 2027. Related Stories News Zhang Yimou To Head Seven-Member Competition Jury At Busan International Film Festival News 'Possible Love' DoP Kim Ji-yong, 'The Blue Road' Director Han Jun-hee & WETA FX's Kimball Thurston Among Speakers For Netflix 'Creative Asia' At BIFF The project marks the tenth anniversary of the original series, one of the titles widely credited with kickstarting the Korean wave internationally. The show closed with a 38.8% nationwide rating; became the first Korean series to air simultaneously in China, where it drew over 2 billion views on iQiyi; and was subsequently sold to more than 30 countries including the U.S., UK, France, Germany, Japan and Russia. Watch on Deadline The Indonesian version reimagines the romance at the heart of the original story through an Indonesian setting and cultural context, while preserving the emotional resonance of the original show. The film is directed by Hanung Bramantyo, one of Indonesia’s leading box-office directors, whose credits include Miracle In Cell No. 7 , also an Indonesian remake of a Korean property, which is the country’s eighth-highest-grossing local film of all time. “Ten years on, Descendants Of The Sun is still one of the titles people point to when they talk about the start of the K-Drama wave,” said Barunson E&A CEO Yoonhee Choi. “We see the strength of the Korean IP as a starting point, not an endpoint. This adaptation places that globally recognized story under a different sun, in an Indonesian landscape with a local sensibility all its own. It retains the familiarity of a story audiences already know and love, while opening it to a new context and, we believe, audiences beyond Indonesia.” Woosik Seo, CEO of Barunson C&C and an executive producer of the film, said: “As the producer behind the original series, I deeply admire how the director has honoured its spirit while creating a truly Indonesian story that I believe will translate just as powerfully wherever it’s seen.” Barunson E&A’s ACFM slate also includes Satan’s Slaves: Origin , the prequel to Joko Anwar’s blockbuster horror franchise; Stoneborn , an occult mystery from the creative team behind Exhuma , starring Jongseo Jeon ( Burning ) and Sul Kyung-gu ( Possible Lo ve); and comedy Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng , which is premiering in Busan International Film Festival and set for theatrical release on October 28.
