title: Paramount Settles Antitrust Case With State AGs, Removing Obstacle to Warner Bros. Deal
full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:56am PT Paramount Settles Antitrust Case With State AGs, Removing Obstacle to Warner Bros. Deal By Gene Maddaus Plus Icon Gene Maddaus Senior Media Writer @GeneMaddaus Latest Paramount Settlement Talks With State AGs Reach Critical Stage as Merger Opponents Rally and Urge Rob Bonta ‘Do Not Cave’ 1 day ago Gavin Newsom Signs Bill Creating $10 Million Post-Production Tax Credit 2 days ago Paramount and California AG Bonta Reportedly in ‘Advanced Talks’ to Settle Antitrust Suit 3 days ago See All Getty Images Paramount has reached a deal with 12 state attorneys general that removes a major obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal comes just before the company was to begin accruing a $7 million daily “ticking fee” on Oct. 1, which was seen as an important milestone in the case. Bloomberg was first to report the news, followed by the Wall Street Journal. A source also confirmed to Variety that a deal is done. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony The merger was on hold pending the outcome of the states’ antitrust lawsuit, which was set for a trial on March 2, 2027. The $111 billion merger is the largest in Hollywood history. Popular on Variety Details of the agreement have yet to be made public. An official announcement is expected to come later Monday. The two sides spent the weekend in tense discussions over Paramount’s commitments to remain in California and over guarantees for its production levels. The discussions also focused on editorial oversight of CBS News and CNN, a key concern for East Coast attorneys general. Sources said the settlement does not require Paramount to make any major divestitures. California Attorney General Rob Bonta led the 12-state coalition, which sued to block the deal in July despite prior approval from the U.S. Department of Justice. Since then, Bonta has insisted on “robust structural remedies” — which has been taken to mean significant divestitures. Opponents of the deal were quick to blast Bonta for “caving” to Paramount’s pressure campaign. “Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored and bullied their way to the top,” said Alvaro Bedoya, a senior advisor at the American Economic Liberties Project, who also expressed disappointment with California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra, who is running for the governor’s seat. “People want champions who are not afraid of rich bullies. Newsom, Becerra and Bonta did not meet that mark. The people who work in the film and TV industry and the small businesses who support it will suffer as a result. And so will everyone who values dissent in our democracy.” The Writers Guild of America filed a separate suit to block the merger in July, and that case was set to be heard along with the states’ case in March. The WGA is expected to sign on to the settlement agreement. Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin, who is overseeing the states’ antitrust case, granted a 28-day restraining order in July, finding that the states had put forward a strong case that the deal would harm competition in the basic cable and theatrical markets. Paramount then agreed to pause the transaction until a trial on the merits, rather than fight a motion for a preliminary injunction. The states argued that the merger would lead to higher prices and fewer options for theaters and cable and satellite providers, who would in turn pass on higher costs to consumers. Paramount has argued all along that the deal is pro-competitive and will result in more content production as the company seeks to take on streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon. In recent weeks, Paramount has sought to ratchet up the pressure on Bonta to abandon the case, including by threatening to leave California and move to Texas or Tennessee. Paramount has also enlisted state Democratic lawmakers to urge Bonta to settle, while IATSE and the Directors Guild of America have also pushed for a deal. Cinema United, the trade group representing theaters, had initially strongly opposed the merger. But as its three largest members — AMC, Cinemark and Regal — came out in favor of a settlement one-by-one, the group also reversed itself and called for a deal. That left Bonta and the other attorneys general in the position of trying to prove economic harm to exhibitors without the support of many of them. title: Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban
full_text: Sep 21, 2026 7:26am PT Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban 1 hour ago Paramount Settlement Talks With States Progress but Some AGs Push for Tougher Terms 14 hours ago White House Blocks CNN and MS NOW Journalists From Entry and Confiscates Their Badges After Donald Trump Bans Networks 2 days ago See All Getty Images In an unprecedented move, four of the five TV networks that provide White House pool coverage of President Donald Trump — ABC News , CBS News , NBC News and Fox News — have joined in solidarity with CNN , which is the fifth TV pooler, announcing they are suspending coverage of the president because of his ban of CNN. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” the five networks said in a joint statement Monday. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Suspended, Position Will Be Recast The blackout of White House pool coverage by the networks comes after the Trump administration suspended CNN as the designated TV pool provider on Monday, Sept. 21 — leaving no TV pooler for the day. It also follows CNN, MS NOW and Politico announcing that they are suing Trump and three White House officials over his unilateral ban of the news outlets, alleging it violates the First Amendment. Popular on Variety The suspension of the TV news pool means that, for the time being, no major television network will provide coverage of Trump’s events, including his scheduled appearances Monday at the White House and his visit to the United Nations in New York City. Bryan Boughton, Fox News’ Washington bureau chief and the current White House TV pool chair, wrote in an email to the other networks Monday, ”This is to advise that, effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President. This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties. There will be no replacement pool put in place.” The White House designates secondary TV news pool providers (as well as those for print, radio and new media outlets). However, the secondary TV networks do not have any obligation to provide content to third parties. Trump said on social media Friday, Sept. 18, that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico “effective immediately” from the White House , citing his familiar allegation that they propagate “fake news.” The White House barred entry to staffers from the three outlets on Saturday and revoked their press passes. At an Oval Office briefing Friday, Trump indicated that there was no single story that triggered him to ban the news outlets, but was rather a cumulative effect of their “purposely negative” coverage. We will provide further updates as this situation develops.” The network boycott of the pool is taking place during an eventful week: Trump is addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. title: Movie Theater Advertising Giant Closes $275 Million Deal to Expand to Offices
full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 7:12am National CineMedia's Noovie pre-show, hosted by Maria Menounos, features trivia, ads and promo interviews. National CineMedia National CineMedia , the in-theater advertising company that works with AMC Theatres, Cinemark and Regal for pre-show commercials content, has closed a major deal to venture outside of the cinema. The firm, led by Thomas Lesinski, has sealed an agreement to acquire Captivate Holdings, which powers tens of thousands of small screens in office buildings, lobbies and elevators that show short ads and content as people walk by (or when waiting for your floor in an elevator). The deal is valued at $275 million. National CineMedia already has a foothold in this business through all of its screens showing ads in movie theater lobbies (it had 17,000 screens in over 1,300 theaters, as of its annual report). Now it wants to bring that formula to office buildings and residential properties, too. And with Captivate’s platform, the company says it’ll have 48,000 digital screens to do so. Its primary vehicle to sell ads is its Noovie pre-show which is hosted by former Today correspondent Maria Menounos and features movie trivia, junket-style interviews with celebrities and Hollywood flashback moments mixed in with commercials. Since emerging from bankruptcy in 2023 — just as the COVID years were particularly brutal to theaters, they also wreaked havoc on in-theater advertising — National CineMedia has been positioning itself for a rebuild. The company spent $8.2 million last November to buy Spotlight Cinema Network, an ad network which caters to boutique, luxury and drive-in theaters like Cinépolis Luxury Cinema, Landmark Theatres and more. The restructured firm, once co-owned and launched by the major theater chains as a joint venture, also disclosed in its annual report that it now has no ownership interest from AMC and Cinemark as of the beginning of this year. Now it’s looking to become a national player in the advertising game, but is taking on debt to do so in the form of a $275 million senior secured first lien term loan facility. National CineMedia bought Captivate from growth equity firm Generation Partners, which had owned the advertising platform since 2013, when it purchased the company from newspaper giant Gannett. “The acquisition of Captivate is a key step in advancing NCM’s strategy to build a broader premium video and digital out-of-home advertising platform,” stated National CineMedia chief Lesinski on Monday, adding: “With the transaction now closed, our focus turns to bringing these capabilities together and executing on the opportunities we see across the combined business.” THR

title: Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review
full_text: Sep 21, 2026 6:15am PT Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Peter Krause’s ‘Line of Fire’ Is a Promising and Engaging NBC Procedural Drama: TV Review 2 hours ago ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Proves the Show Just Wouldn’t Work Without Tom Hardy 3 days ago Netflix’s ‘Monster’ Finally Delivers an Outrageously Engaging Season With ‘The Lizzie Borden Story’: TV Review 4 days ago See All NBC For decades, law-enforcement procedurals have been staples on television, and when they are done well, these series build loyal fanbases that stick with them for years. NBC ’s newest drama, “ Line of Fire ” is from “Quantico” creator Joshua Safran and loosely based on executive producer Jenna Bush Hager’s experiences with the United States Secret Service. The show has all the makings of becoming a classic in the canon of beloved police procedurals. “Line of Fire” follows the Hollingsworth family: Secret Service Agent Mike Hollingsworth ( Peter Krause ); his estranged wife, U.S. Marshal Jane Hollingsworth ( Hope Davis ); and their three adult children, FBI Agent Clare Hollingsworth (Kat Cunning), Secret Service Agent Mike “Micah” Hollingsworth Jr. (Tommy O’Brien) and DOJ analyst Russ Hollingsworth (Taylor Bloom). Mike, Jane and their children try to keep things professional, but continually cross personal boundaries because of their agencies’ proximity. Boasting intense family dynamics and several truly intriguing cases, “Line of Fire” has a depth, intensity and a hint of soapiness that works perfectly within the genre. Related Stories 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Allegedly Visited Pedophilia Chatroom, Leading to Suspension 'Wheel of Fortune' Announcer Jim Thornton Fired by Sony The 10-episode first season (two episodes were available for review) opens in Crozet, Virginia. A U.S. Marshal, under the guise of being a delivery driver, attempts to track down a missing fugitive. Unfortunately, before the morning breaks, both the Marshal and the outlaw lay dead in the woods. The next day, Jane arrives at the crime scene, determined to figure out what happened. Needing a bit more reach than the Marshals can offer, Jane calls in her daughter, Clare, for her expertise and for the FBI’s resources. Though Clare is eager to help, Jane’s team is not exactly pleased that the FBI is encroaching on her territory. For her part, Clare isn’t thrilled when her mother badgers her about bringing her mysterious new boyfriend to dinner to finally meet the family. Popular on Variety Back in Washington, D.C., Mike is set to finish out his final week at the Secret Service Headquarters before retiring. Yet, he’s increasingly concerned Micah is skirting his professional duties for a personal relationship with Sydney (Savannah Lee Smith), the president’s college-age daughter. Elsewhere, Russell is ready to get his feet wet at the DOJ, but his family’s constant requests complicate his role. Chaos and dysfunction are par for the course for the Hollingsworths. But when a seemingly standard case unearths long-buried secrets that threaten the family’s safety, each person must decide whether their jobs are worth more than the people they love. From bank robberies to cartel killings and even contending with the First Family’s drama in the White House, all of the cases the Hollingsworths handle are interesting. Still, the Hollingsworth family dynamic anchors “Line of Fire.” Though they’ve been long separated, Jane and Mike have a solid friendship; one that can only be formed after knowing and loving someone intimately for half your life. Not only do the former couple share children, but Mike and Jane also share secrets — shocking ones they keep close to their chests. The siblings, each with unique relationships with their parents and each other, are also well mapped out. Though only two episodes were available to screen, the family feels well lived-in: a boisterous clan with varied personalities becomes the ecosystem that shapes the series. In the pilot, Mike and the siblings arrive at Jane’s house for a chaotic and hilarious family dinner to meet the beau Clare has avoided introducing them to. Immediately, the audience gets a full sense of who these people are and how this family functions. Yet, that doesn’t make any of the cases sprinkled within the show any less worthwhile. In fact, it makes the conspiracy sitting at the center of “Line of Fire” even more gripping. “Line of Fire” has all of the essential elements that make procedural dramas so fun. With a stellar cast and some detailed mysteries which will likely stretch across the season (and into the next, assuming there is one), changing the Hollingsworth family dynamic as we know it, it’s clear NBC has a gem on its hands. “Line of Fire” debuts Sept. 21 on NBC, with the remaining episodes airing weekly on Mondays. title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico Sue White House for Revoking Press Credentials: “Patently Unconstitutional”
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 5:03am The White House Briefing room, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC Photo by Graeme Sloan/Getty Images CNN , MS NOW and Politico are suing the Trump administration after the White House revoked their press credentials, effectively banning them from the White House complex and making it a challenge to cover the President and his staff. “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes,” the three news outlets said in a statement early Monday morning. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Related Stories Business Sylvester Stallone Learned About Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship While Watching TV: "It Won't Work" TV Alan Ritchson Reveals Which 'Reacher' Season Got Canceled After "Someone Got Re-Elected" In fact, CNN had been slated to be the primary TV press pool Monday, a day in which President Trump is slated to fly to New York for meetings with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. In a memo later Monday morning, the White House TV pool had been suspended given CNN’s banishment. CNN splits the primary pool duties with ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government,” a joint statement from TV pool companies said. “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.” In their lawsuit (led by famed First Amendment litigator Ted Boutrous), the news outlets argue that Trump’s decision was in profound conflict with the law. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit states. “Presidents from the earliest days of the Republic have disagreed with and complained about the tenor and content of press coverage of their administrations. But as the Supreme Court has recognized, the First Amendment, including its guarantee of a free press, reflects “a profound national commitment to the principle that debate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and that it may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials.” The suit states quoting a passage from the landmark case, New York Times Co . v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 270 (1964). “And the Constitution protects the liberty and property interests that news organizations and White House reporters have in their press credentials and the access those credentials afford them to cover the White House for the benefit of the public,” it continues. “No official can deprive Plaintiffs of those interests on a whim—with no notice, no process, and no warning—as the President did here.” Trump announced his ban in a post Friday , causing some confusion in the White House as crews from the outelts remained onsite. However, on Saturday morning journalists from all three outlets trying to enter the White House complex found that their credentials had been revoked . In an Oval Office appearance, Trump said that the decision followed cumulative coverage over the past few years, and wasn’t driven by any story in particular. “The President repeated his straightforward rationale for targeting these three news organizations, calling it ‘wrong’ to ‘allow people to write purposely negative stories,'” the lawsuit recounts. “The President complained about coverage he considers ‘one-sided’ and ‘never good,’ and at one point even referred to his own unprecedented act as the ‘ban on the free press.'” He also suggested that he knew his move would end up being litigated, suggesting that the outcome would depend on the judge that gets the cse. In his first term the White House banned CNN correspondent Jim Acosta from the White House, but a judge ordered his pass returned, citing First Amendment protections. The AP had also sued after it was barred from covering certain events after its style guide declined to refer to the body of water as the Gulf of America. THR

title: CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted CNN, MS NOW And Politico To Sue Donald Trump Over His White House Ban CNN, MS NOW And Politico Journalists Denied White House Entry; Colleagues Condemn Trump’s Ban Judge Says Kennedy Center Must Give Court 30 Days Notice Of Any Demolition Plans After Trump Floats Prospect It Could Be “Ripped Down” View All September 21, 2026 3:43am Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images UPDATED: CNN , Politico and MS NOW are suing Donald Trump and other White House officials after the president banned him from the complex. In the lawsuit, the news outlets are asking a federal judge to immediately restore their access, which was denied on Saturday, a day after Trump announced he was restricting them from entry to the White House grounds. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.” The new organizations said in a joint statement, “This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes. “Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” Related Stories Politics Sylvester Stallone Told Trump Hollywood Ambassadorship Was "Impossible" But Was Appointed Anyway: "It Won't Work" News Alan Ritchson On The 'Reacher' Season That Was Canceled After "Someone Got Re-Elected" The White House also removed CNN from the White House pool on Monday, the day it was scheduled to be the primary network for their coverage. As a result, there will be no TV pool on a day when Trump is traveling to New York, signaling that other networks declined to serve as replacements because of the president’s targeting of CNN. Watch on Deadline The news outlets state in their lawsuit, “The President banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and the individual reporters covering the news for those media organizations, in disregard of the most basic guarantees of the First Amendment and the Due Process Clause. He did so expressly for the improper purpose of retaliating against Plaintiffs for past news coverage because he deemed it ‘negative’ and chilling future reporting about him and his administration’s policies and actions. “President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration. But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting. The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained.” The lawsuit claims violation of the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause and First Amendment retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. The outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order and injunction to prohibit the ban from being enforced and to require that their access be restored, as well as a declaratory ruling. The outlets are represented from Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represented CNN’s Jim Acosta when his credentials were revoked in Trump’s first term, as well as others at Gibson Dunn, including Katie Townsend and Patrick Fuster. In addition to the impact of the ban on their own news organizations, the outlets argue in the lawsuit that it “inflicts an injury on all news media organizations—who now risk a similar fate if they engage in reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable. And the public at large suffers for however long the unconstitutional ban restricts access to current and complete information about their government. These irreparable harms should not be tolerated for a day longer. The Court should immediately enjoin enforcement of the ban.” The lawsuit also names White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, Secret Service Director Sean Curran and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. Shortly after the lawsuit was announced, Trump posted on Truth Social, “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America. It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” In 2018, in the case of Acosta, a federal judge ruled that precedent required that the White House give proper notice of a revocation. In the 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” The White House has yet to provide a legal justification for revoking the credentials of the news outlets. On ABC’s This Week on Sunday, host Jon Karl pressed House Majority Leader Steve Scalise on Trump’s ban. “Do you support him banning these news organizations because he doesn’t like what they are reporting?” Karl asked. Scalise deflected, pointing to Trump’s accessibility to the media and claimed that Joe Biden removed the press credentials from more than 400 news organizations. In fact, the Biden White House established new criteria for credentialing, based in part on how often holders had used the hard passes and that they had full time employment and residency in the D.C. area. It was not based on a news organization’s viewpoint, although the changes were made after one correspondent had repeatedly interrupted press briefings. Karl told Scalise that they “were not banned from the White House.” He then asked Scalise whether Trump’s ban violates the First Amendment, but Scalise again did not answer. Karl moved on to another topic. title: Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Cancels  2026 Edition
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain Israeli Film Council Calls For Festivals To Be Removed From Funding Criteria & Creation Of Strand For Films Celebrating Israeli Soldiers Amid ‘NAZA’ Firestorm Oscars: France Selects ‘Minotaur’ For Best International Feature Film Race View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Alessandra Ambrosio attends the Closing Night red carpet at the Red Sea International Film Festival 2025 Getty images Saudi Arabia ‘s Red Sea Film Foundation has cancelled the 2026 edition of the Red Sea International Film Festival , saying in a statement that the sixth edition had been postponed to the fourth quarter of 2027. The announcement follows weeks of speculation over whether the 2026 edition, scheduled to unfold from December 3-12 in the Red Sea port city of Jeddah, would take place amid tensions across the entire Gulf region due to the U.S.-Israeli-Iran war. Aside from retaliatory strikes on neighboring territories, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman, Iran has also sought to take control of the Strait of Hormuz connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, a key shipping route for their oil and other goods. Related Stories Festivals Dubai Film Festival To Return In December 2027, As 2026 Edition Of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Film Festival Looks Uncertain News Saudi Arabia To Invest $7 Billion In Three Theme Parks Near Paris Beyond direct threats from Iran, Saudi Arabia is also dealing with a flareup in its conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi group in recent weeks. Watch on Deadline The foundation did not mention the geopolitical tensions saying rather that the decision “followed a comprehensive review of a range of considerations relating to the timing of the next edition, including the logistical requirements involved in staging an international event of this scale.” Since the event’s launch in 2021, in the wake of Saudi Arabia’s lifting of its 35-year cinema ban at the end of 2017, it has grown into the Gulf region’s main film festival with a steady flow of high-profile Hollywood guests, burgeoning industry events, and wide Middle East and international participation. Aside from geopolitical tensions beyond its control, the festival has also been subject to internal debate about its future direction in recent months. In June, the foundation’s longtime Managing Director Shivani Pandya Malhotra, who helped spearhead the launch of the festival having joined the body in 2019, stepped down with a number of her close team members leaving as well. In the backdrop, there are also wider questions around Saudi Arabia’s larger commitment to the film industry, with the country’s entertainment focus shifting to the video game sector and sports such as boxing and soccer. The foundation made it clear in its statement that the festival will be back for sixth edition in 2027 with “a renewed vision and a programme that continues to celebrate cinema and filmmakers from Saudi Arabia, the region and around the world.” It also emphasized that it will continue its year-round mission of supporting filmmakers and strengthening the film industries through the Red Sea Fund, Red Sea Labs and its wider programmes and initiatives. As part of this continued commitment, the foundation said it will introduce year-round programming at Culture Square in Jeddah from November 2026, establishing it as an ongoing destination for film screenings, cultural events and specialised film-industry programmes. “The Red Sea Film Foundation extends its sincere appreciation to filmmakers, partners, guests and audiences for their continued trust and support. We look forward to welcoming the global film community back to Historic Jeddah in 2027 for a sixth edition that celebrates cinema, creativity and cultural dialogue,” concluded its statement. In the meantime, Gulf neighbor the United Arab Emirates announced last week that it is reviving the Dubai International Film Festival following a 10-year hiatus, with a scheduled December 8, 2027 opening date, which could see it clash with the Red Sea. In the backdrop, Qatar’s Doha Film Festival is pushing on with plans for its second edition running this November 19-27, 2026. title: “It Fills Me With Pride”: How the Basque Country Is Nurturing Its Next Generation of Filmmakers
full_text: × Skip to main content Breaking News Paramount, 12 States to Settle Warner Bros. Megamerger Fight close By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 21, 2026 3:00am Nitya López Saitua on the set of 'Family Drill.' San Sebastián Film Festival It’s no longer a secret that Basque cinema is getting some overdue time in the spotlight. Thanks to an almighty production boom in the region, powered by a whopping 60 percent tax rebate (increasing to 70 percent for projects shot in the Basque language, Euskera), the Basque Country’s film and TV output has never looked so healthy. And the proof is in the pudding: The Hollywood Reporter took an in-depth look at the record 45 nominations for Basque projects at this year’s Goyas, also known as “the Spanish Oscars,” after a decade of concentrated investment. Related Stories Movies Red Sea Film Festival Cancels 2026 Edition, Vows to Return Next Year With "Renewed Vision" Movies San Sebastian Winner Yesim Ustaoglu Returns to Competition With 'What Remains' (Exclusive Clip) With San Sebastián’s profile rising exponentially every September, the people working behind the scenes to make sure Basque cinema is capitalizing on every single success are already pushing the next generation of original voices into the festival hot seat. At the 74th edition, a total of 31 titles with Basque production ties — including David Pérez Sañudo’s hotly anticipated competition title The Harvester — will screen across the festival’s many selections. Twelve are documentaries, marking a real moment for Basque docs at this installment. But with award statuettes firmly on the mantel, the Basque region now sets itself the task of sustaining this run of form long-term. The answer? Find and nurture the next generation’s emerging talent. For example, the debut feature from Nitya López Saitua in Zinemira, Family Drill , a project fuelled by word-of-mouth buzz across northern Spain . “He’s been doing great as a first AD and second AD for so many years,” begins Mar Izquierdo, coordinator of Zineuskadi, a non-profit operating at the epicentre of the Basque film and TV industry, “and everyone was like, ‘But he’s got it. He’s not going to be an AD.’ And we really do hope that with this film, everyone else will be able to see it.” Izquierdo’s company works strategically to promote the Basque audiovisual sector, partnering with every production output in the region, working alongside the Basque government’s culture department and public broadcaster ETB Basque to help facilitate co-productions, distribution and sales deals, as well as earning key projects coveted slots at the globe’s biggest film festivals and plotting awards campaigns. One young talent they’ve thrown their support behind is the 30-year-old López, who was in such a hurry to capture the creative process practically spilling out of his head that Family Drill — a co-production with Mubox Studio, who are distributing the film — was shot with just 10 people across three days in his childhood home on the Basque coast. He tells THR : “Iraia Elias and Miguel Garcés [play] my mom and dad and we recreate my parents’ relationship, [leading up to] the last argument that broke the relationship when I was four years old.” It is as deeply personal as it sounds. “This was a way to recreate memories that I didn’t have,” says López, firmly out of AD mode and in full-fledged director mode. “And I think it was very important to free-work on the scenes, without a script.” Family Drill San Sebastian Film Festival López’s determination to start the shoot before he lost that powerful sense of direction in chronicling his parents’ split speaks to the strength of the Basque Country’s storytelling. “We have really great directors here in the Basque Country, and internationally they are [getting] more recognized,” continues the first-time filmmaker. “I have the opportunity of working with many of them, and I love their work, and I’m very proud to be part of the next generation making movies. I think that we are in a great moment [compared to] making movies here 20 years ago.” It used to be the case that, “if [creatives] want to direct, they must go to other places, go to Madrid,” he explains. Here in the region López calls home, there have never been so many reasons to put roots down. One of his countrymen, Javier Giner, also arrives at the San Sebastián Film Festival with his first movie. This Solitude is premiering in the New Directors section. A debut feature it may technically be, but director-writer Giner has known global success with the International Emmy-winning I, Addict series, based on his own life and struggle with drug addiction. With This Solitude , Giner, who grew up in Bilbao, reacts to the unprecedented impact of that show. “ I, Addict was a huge hit in Spain and it dealt with a part of my life where I suffered [with] the illness of addiction,” he says. “After that explosive TV series where I presented myself to the world with no mask, I needed to go back to my childhood, to a very intimate place, a very silent place — much smaller than I, Addict .” Giner suddenly found himself shooting where he grew up, Bilbao, back to the places and locations that he says “have an emotional resonance” for him. The film, starring Oriol Pla, Marina Salas, Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz and Itziar Lazkano, is a Balance Media Entertainment production, with The Embassy TV and Basajaun Filmak as co-producers, and Filmax handling distribution. “We meet two young people who live in Bilbao, Leo and Lorea, and we follow them through the grief process after they break a five-year-long relationship,” Giner explains. “And I use that journey as an excuse to talk about a lot of things like class, the housing [crisis]. […] Those moments in our lives everyone goes through, in a sense of reconstructing yourself because nothing works around you and you don’t quite grasp who you are [or] what you want.” He speaks with as much gusto as López, who also, in some way, depicts his Basque youth on screen — a common theme running through many of these films — and seeing fellow regional filmmakers make a name for themselves in recent years only speaks to the urgency of the stories coming out of the Basque Country, according to Giner. “To be honest, it fills me with pride,” he says. “I think movies and filmmakers, when they’re honest with their upbringing and their roots, there’s something very beautiful in it. As an audience member, I love when I discover London through Mike Leigh’s eyes, for example, or I discover parts of the world that I don’t know about through some filmmaker’s eyes.” Giner says that in the last 10 years, especially, Basque stories have been “very important to tell.” He continues: “I jokingly call This Solitude my very Basque movie, because there’s a reflection of identity in the movie… It tells [you] a lot about the place. And the Basque Country, it’s beautiful. It has beautiful landscapes. It has great possibilities. It is filled with really talented people, both in front of and behind the camera. So, I mean, it fills me with total pride if someone considers me the representation of the Basque Country at this year’s festival.” He is admittedly still pinching himself that he’s here: “It’s incredible. To be honest, a lot of my film education has to do with the San Sebastián Film Festival because when I was a teenager, I used to go from Bilbao to San Sebastián and watch movies.” López concurs that Basque cinema has its own culture, but also lauds the region’s directors for still being able to make “really universal movies.” And Izquierdo says the variation across the projects this year is particularly exciting for her. “The best thing is we are covering every possible subject,” she says. “We have a biopic for a musical group. We have culinary cinema. We have a French co-production, a coming-of-age [film] within a school. We have everything.” Basque filmmaker Javier Giner. San Sebastian Film Festival And naturally, the festival also serves as something of a springboard for those nail-biting awards runs. “It’s the most important film festival in Spain and one of the [category] A film festivals in the world,” says Giner about what a premiere in San Sebastián can do for one’s Goya hopes. “So it’s definitely a great trampoline. But it’s something that I don’t want to think about because I don’t want to get lost in that narrative and it take away from the pure pleasure of putting a film out there and sharing it with the public.” Of course, it’s not just Basque filmmakers travelling to shoot here. Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang is presenting Dust in San Sebastián, a short film and exhibition piece as part of his Walker series, which is a Basque co-production. Nanni Moretti made the most of those tempting tax incentives, too, with his last movie It Will Happen Tonight filming in the region before its recent Venice Film Festival premiere, and the Catherine Zeta-Jones starrer Kill Jackie — releasing Oct. 2 — shot extensively across Bilbao. “It’s not only that we continue to have emerging talent, but we are able to co-produce and have A-class films as minority co-producers,” beams Izquierdo. But she maintains that the most rewarding part of her job is platforming the next generation of Basque filmmakers, who are carving out a path by leading with instinct, leaning into personal storytelling, and celebrating each milestone. “The big names know how to [make] their way through the other festivals,” says Izquierdo. “But some of them need this in order to get the next one — it’s a window of opportunity for them, because otherwise maybe their documentary or small film would be just another small fish in the pond. Here,” she adds, “they get the chance on the big screen, where exhibitors and distributors will be able to notice them.” The 2026 San Sebastián International Film Festival runs Sep. 18-26. THR

title: Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News Done! Paramount Settles Antitrust Suit, Set To Seal Deal For Warner Bros. Discovery Read the full story By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse BBC Drama ‘Ministry Of Time’ Adds Adeel Akhtar, Ciaran Hinds & Eight More To Cast Eagle Eye Drama Acquires ‘The Great Dictator’, Matthew Sweet’s Biography Of Barbara Cartland Princess Di Returns To ‘SNL UK’ As “Deeply Intelligent, Autonomous, Neurokinetic Android” In Cold Open Skewering King Charles, Ed Sheeran & AI View All September 21, 2026 2:29am 'The Great Dictator' ITV Studios EXCLUSIVE: Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to The Great Dictator , Matthew Sweet ‘s biography of the flamboyant and eccentric late Dame Barbara Cartland . Historian, novelist and screenwriter Sweet’s book tells the story of author known as ‘The Queen of Romance’ Cartland, who was one of the UK’s most recognizable figures across the 20th century. She was famous for dressing in pink and taking her Pekinese dogs with her wherever she went. Born in 1901, Cartland was a fixture of British high society, rubbing shoulders with press barons, politicians, the aristocracy and the Royal Family, as step-grandmother to Princess Diana. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals Mark Gatiss Drama 'Bookish' Returning For Third Chapter & Festive Special Acquisitions HBO Max Buys Mark Gatiss Series 'Bookish' For Australia As Sales Pass The 100-Territory Mark Bookish co-writer Sweet’s book, published this month by Hodder & Stoughton, is the result of years of research into her life. It has been positively reviewed by the likes of The Guardian, The Times and documentarian Louis Theroux, and ITV Studios-owned Eagle Eye will now look to adapt the story of the ‘woman in pink’, whose romance novels sold close to a billion copies in 38 languages. Watch on Deadline Eagle Eye Drama CEO Walter Iuzzolino said: “Matthew Sweet gained unparalleled access to the Cartland family archives, and what he has uncovered is a story more compelling and unbelievable than her most outlandish plots, which will provide a wonderful bedrock to build an unmissable scripted series.” Eagle Eye CCO Jo McGrath added that Cartland was the third-biggest selling author of all time, behind only William Shakespeare and Agatha Christie, adding she would be a “gift of a role for a great actress.” “Known for her outlandish pink chiffon clothes and thick Meltonian black shoe cream mascara, she is a figure who has been loved and scorned in equal measure,” said McGrath. “She was a ferocious champion of romantic love with a less than idyllic and rather scandalous love life of her own. “A friend of Winston Churchill, she dined with Margaret Thatcher – to whom she prescribed alternative remedies and oxygen supplements – and of course the step-grandmother to Princess Diana, who loved her books as a young woman.” Sweet, whose series Bookish is produced through Eagle Eye, said: “I feel like I’ve been caught up in a pink chiffon whirlwind in the last few days, with the reviews and the Baillie Gifford longlist. Now Eagle Eye Drama has acquired the rights to bring The Great Dictator to television. They are the perfect producers and I know they will bring Barbara’s world to life with impeccable style.” Eagle Eye is arguably best known for Bookish , the light crime series in which Mark Gatiss plays a closeted post-war detective. It was renewed for a third season and festive special last month. The production house also makes Channel 4’s The Couple Next Door and the high-rating Patience and Ben Miller drama Professor T for ITV. It is also adapting ITV’s forthcoming Richard Armitage crime series Winter after secured the rights to the book. Tom Perrin, Editorial Consultant, Hodder & Stoughton, noted The Great Dictator had been “a runaway success” since publication and had been longlisted for the Baillie Gifford Prize. Cartland’s life has been the subject of many documentaries, while Anne Reid starred as the author in the BBC’s 2008 telemovie In Love with Barbara .
